title: Why Do Indians Overspend at Diwali? What 2026 Data Shows

content:
Indians overspend at Diwali because the brain treats festival season as a separate mental budget, not the same pool as everyday money. That's called mental accounting, and every human does it. But in 2026, BNPL apps and no-cost EMIs have turbocharged the tendency, with credit-based festive purchases up roughly 50% year over year.

Key Takeaways

  • India's festive window (Navratri to Diwali 2025) generated Rs 6.05 lakh crore in trade, a 25% jump from 2024.
  • Credit-on-UPI and BNPL usage rose about 50% during the 2025 festive peak.
  • Mental accounting makes festival money feel different from regular money, loosening normal spending guardrails.
  • No-cost EMI is rarely free: the cost is usually baked into the product price or the card's annual fee.
  • October credit often becomes January stress. That's the cycle worth breaking.

Why Do Indians Overspend at Diwali?

Mental accounting is the main reason. When the brain assigns income to a 'Diwali fund' or treats a festive bonus as windfall, it relaxes the usual spending guardrails. That's why buying a TV at Diwali feels different from buying one in March, even if your income and the price tag are identical. The calendar changes the psychology, not the math.

The festive bonus reinforces this loop. When your employer hands you money in October specifically because it's Diwali, your brain books it as 'festival money.' Spending it feels appropriate, even obligatory. Saving it feels like missing the point. This has occured in Indian households for generations, long before EMIs existed.

There's also genuine social weight. Gifting at Diwali isn't just nice, it's expected. Companies send boxes to vendors. Families give sweets to neighbours. In-laws notice. A big chunk of the overspend isn't self-indulgence. It's social obligation wearing a nice wrapper.

What Does 2026 Festive Spending Data Show?

India's festive retail window in 2025 generated Rs 6.05 lakh crore in trade between Navratri and Diwali, a 25% jump from the year before. UPI transactions hit Rs 87,569 crore per day during Diwali's three-day peak. And 95% of consumers said they planned to spend more in the 2026 festive season, even with inflation running above average.

Premium products are climbing fastest. TVs above Rs 35,000 sold at twice the rate of the previous year during the same period. Vehicle registrations hit 33.57 lakh in the Navratri-to-Diwali window, up 17% from 2024. And ecommerce EMI transactions rose 50% from the year before.

That last number is the one worth sitting with.

Does No-Cost EMI Actually Cost Nothing?

Almost never. Retailers either inflate the base price before applying the 'no cost' scheme, or the offer applies only to specific credit cards that carry annual fees. The cost is real. It's just not labeled as interest. You're paying. It just looks different on the screen.

When a Rs 1,00,000 TV becomes 20 monthly payments of Rs 5,000, your brain stops comparing the price to your savings. It compares it to your monthly cash flow. That's the mechanism BNPL apps exploit deliberately. Behavioral economists call this temporal discounting: small future payments feel less real than money in your hand right now. The brain systematically underweights them.

BNPL has made this frictionless. Credit-on-UPI, LazyPay, and card-based EMIs let you split a purchase in under three seconds, before any reflection has a chance to kick in. When the gap between impulse and transaction collapses to one tap, it's convienient for the seller and expensive for you.

When Is Diwali Spending Actually a Problem?

Festive spending is fine when it comes from savings or a planned budget. It becomes a problem when you're borrowing for consumption items rather than assets, and when repayments cut into the following months' savings rate. The pattern to watch: if you're still paying October's EMIs in March, it's not a deal, it's debt.

Many households don't keep their festive spending and regular expenses in seperate mental boxes, and that's how October becomes March's problem. A workable rule: any festive purchase you can't pay off within 30 days of your card statement closing is debt by any honest definition, regardless of what the app calls it. If you're managing serious debt already, a certified financial planner will give better guidance than any general rule.

Worth knowing: some festive spending makes real sense. A fridge you'd have bought in January anyway, purchased now at a genuine discount, is just good timing. The problem is the stuff nobody needed until a notification said 40% off and no-cost EMI available.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Diwali spending good or bad for India's economy?

It's mostly good in aggregate: Rs 6.05 lakh crore in festive trade creates real jobs and tax revenue. The risk is at the household level, where impulse credit can create debt that drags savings rates for 6 to 12 months after the festival. Good for GDP, potentially costly for individual balance sheets.

How much should you actually spend at Diwali?

A workable benchmark: total festive spending, including gifts, decor, and celebrations, should stay under one month's take-home income. If you receive a festive bonus, spending up to that amount on festival-specific items is reasonable. Spending above the bonus on credit is where the math starts to hurt.

Is no-cost EMI ever genuinely free?

Rarely. Most no-cost EMI offers are funded by subvention from the manufacturer or retailer, meaning the cost is baked into the list price. If you can negotiate a cash discount of 5 to 8% on the same item, the EMI was not free. Genuine cashback-funded deals exist but are uncommon.

Does BNPL affect your credit score in India?

Yes, if reported to credit bureaus. Most major BNPL providers in India now report to CIBIL or Experian. A missed BNPL payment shows up like any other default. This changed around 2022 to 2023, when many BNPL products were still unregulated. Check the terms before you split any purchase.

How do I avoid Diwali debt without looking cheap on gifts?

Set a gift budget in September, before the ads start. Fixed amounts per tier, like close family, extended family, and colleagues, make the decisions easier. Most recipients notice the thought, not the price. And most people who'd judge your gift budget aren't worth the debt you'd carry to please them.

The Short Version

India spends big at Diwali because the brain genuinely treats festival money as a different category, and BNPL makes it cheaper to start and more expensive to finish. The data is clear: festive credit use is climbing 50% year over year while incomes aren't.

Festive spending isn't the problem. Unplanned festive debt is. The difference is whether you know your number before the sale starts.
